conventions: The possessive formula runs through this chapter in four shapes, and each is read by what stands in the clause (rule 43). v. 3 writes הָיוּ, so the verb takes the *had*, the preposition לוֹ is unrepresented under rule 40, the suffix takes the subject *he*, and the clause's לֹא takes the determiner *no* under rule 15. vv. 4, 9, 10 are verbless: אַיִן takes *no* under rule 50, the לְ takes *have* or *had*, and the suffix takes *he*. v. 8 is the same verbless clause, but the ASV writes no subject pronoun there — the subject carries over from *a man* — so the suffix is unrepresented under rule 22; that is not a split with vv. 9-10, and the difference is the ASV's, not the analysis's. v. 11 writes the possessor אָבִיו, which takes the English subject noun *his father* while the suffix keeps only *his* and the לְ still carries the *have*. v. 17 is a relative possessive: the written אֲשֶׁר supplies the English subject, the לְ takes *have*, אַיִן takes *no*, and the resumptive suffix takes nothing.

*Take thee* (v. 18) and *Get thee up* (v. 12) are placed by what the Hebrew writes rather than by the English they share. v. 18 writes לְךָ, so the preposition is unrepresented under rule 40 and the suffix takes the *thee* under rule 18. v. 12 writes no dative at all, and its *thee* is kept inside the imperative's own unit as part of the ASV's fixed rendering of the verb of motion, on the ground that it supplies no argument the Hebrew lacks but is coreferential with the imperative's own subject; the competing reading marks it `added` under rule 44's supplied-object sentence, whose stated licence is the source verb's voice or elative sense. Nothing else in the chapter folds a supplied pronoun into a verb, and this convention is not authority to do so elsewhere.
report: Read all 23 verses end to end against the 43-lemma candidate table. Every multi-treatment bucket is accounted for by what the ASV writes or by a difference the source carries, so no construction is analysed two ways with nothing in the Hebrew to license it. No patch.

The possessive paradigm is the chapter's densest recurrence (vv. 3, 4, 8, 9, 10, 11, 17) and is consistent under rule 43: v. 3 writes הָיוּ, so the verb takes *had* and לוֹ goes unrepresented; the verbless אֵין clauses put *no* on אַיִן and *have*/*had* on לְ; v. 11 writes the possessor אָבִיו, which takes the English subject noun while the suffix keeps only *his*; v. 17's relative clause gives the subject to the written אֲשֶׁר and leaves the resumptive suffix nothing. The one apparent split — v. 8's unrepresented suffix beside vv. 9-10's *he* — is the ASV writing no subject pronoun in v. 8, the subject carrying over from *a man*. Recorded as a convention so a later reader does not re-open it.

The other recurring constructions are uniform: לִפְנֵי fused to *before* and headed on פָּנֶה in nine places (vv. 2 x3, 5, 17 x2, 19 x2, 21 x2, 22 x2); כַּאֲשֶׁר fused and headed on the governing כְּ in five (vv. 11, 13, 14, 22, 23), rendered *as* four times and *because* once, which is lexis and not analysis; בְּתוֹךְ fused in vv. 3, 4, 7 while v. 4's מִתּוֹךְ is split, correctly, since *from* and *among* are each spent on one morpheme and rule 30's one-rendering condition is unmet. Multi-level chains (vv. 2, 11, 12, 20) supply a *the* at each construct level where no article morpheme stands, and vv. 14, 16, 21 all give the written *the* to a present article on the rectum. עֵדָה as *company* (v. 3) versus *congregation* (v. 17) is ASV lexis over identical structure.

Checked the dimension the lemma table is blind to — supplied English with no source token. The chapter has one `added` unit, v. 11's italic *and* of *a statute and ordinance*, and nothing elsewhere folds a coordinator into a neighbouring unit. The other supplied words are each licensed by a morpheme: determiners under rules 15 and 29, the copulas of vv. 1 and 14 under rule 20, the light-verb complements *a charge* of vv. 19 and 23 and *cause to pass* of vv. 7 and 8 under rule 44, the adverbial-accusative *at*/*in* of vv. 2 and 14 under rule 33, the *Let* of v. 16 under rule 17, and the *both* of v. 21 under rule 14, where the ASV writes the opening correlative before the first member and הוּא is not itself what *both* says.

BSB: all 16 disagreements are documented convention differences, none an error. Seven are unrendered לְ — the לֵאמֹר of vv. 2, 6, 8, 15 (rule 27), the possessive לְ of v. 3 left silent by the written הָיוּ (rules 40, 43), the dative of v. 7 and the ethical dative of v. 18 (rule 40), and the resultative לְחֻקַּת of v. 11 (rule 21). Three are object markers (rule 16), one is the cohortative he of תְּנָה in v. 4 (rule 32), two are suffixes for which the ASV writes no pronoun (vv. 8, 18), two are the determiner morphemes of הַר הָעֲבָרִים הַזֶּה, whose single written determiner *this* belongs to the demonstrative pronoun (rule 41), one is v. 13's second waw, whose *also* answers to the written גַּם, and one is the resumptive suffix of v. 17's relative possessive (rules 22, 43).

Promotions: none. The one judgment sitting at a rule's edge is v. 12's *thee* in *Get thee up*, kept inside the imperative's unit though no dative morpheme is written; rule 44's stated licence for a reflexive is the source verb's own voice or elative sense, which a Qal imperative does not supply. I recorded it as a convention rather than amending rule 44, because no corpus evidence for the construction was before me and widening that rule's reflexive exception on the strength of one token would loosen its supplied-object test for every chapter aligned afterwards. The verse's own note already names the competing `added` reading under rule 8.
